newsitem.title: UK: Bombing brings fears for Northern Irish ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Bombing brings fears for Northern Irish ceasefire.

text.p: Police, politicians and residents of Northern Ireland fear that a Protestant guerrilla ceasefire may have come to end with a weekend bomb attack that injured a Catholic activist.
No group claimed immediate responsibility for the attack which slightly injured Eddie Copeland, a 25-year-old known for his support of the pro-Irish Republican cause.

But politicians on both side of the Northern Irish political divide said it looked like Protestant "loyalist" guerrillas were taking revenge after IRA gunmen wounded a policeman at a Belfast children's hospital on Friday. The policeman had been guarding a Protestant Unionist politician.
"I think it is potentially the beginning of a spiral," said David Ervine of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) political arm of the outlawed pro-British Ulster Volunteer Force.
"I think the peace process is gone," Alex Maskey, a local councillor for Sinn Fein, political wing of the Irish Republican Army, told Independent Television news.
Before matching an IRA ceasefire in October 1994, loyalist extremists would have taken their vengeance with bloody attacks against customers in a Catholic pub or shop.
But they have been praised for their restraint in not reverting to such tactics when IRA guerrillas broke their 17-month ceasefire in February.
"We are waiting for confirmation and I'd rather withhold judgment until then," said the PUP's Billy Hutchinson.
"But obviously it's a matter of concern and what worries me most is that this is not an isolated incident and there could be more to follow. I just hope that is not the case."

British police and security sources have been warning of IRA attacks in the Christmas season. There is little hope the IRA will reinstate the ceasefire any time soon -- and this would be the only move that would allow them to join multi-party peace talks on the future of the province.

Loyalist groups are taking part in the talks, which resume in January. But their places at the table could be jeopardised if the guerrillas on their side of the conflict over British rule of the province return to the gun.
"I have apprehension in relation to the risk that is now apparent in Northern Ireland," said Irish Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Dick Spring.

"I would hope that both sides will have restraint in the coming days. I certainly hope people will listen. The one thing we do not want to do is get back to the tit-for-tat killings that we had in Northern Ireland down through the years."
Only a few hundred people turned out for a peace rally in central Belfast on Sunday, but it was not clear if cold weather or a gloomy atmosphere kept them away.
"Things are at the white-knuckle stage," said one Protestant man on his way to church.
